w: August 1833: Parliament voted freedom for the empire’s enslaved people, paying a vast fortune in compensation to former owners rather than to the freed.

March 1867: Secretary Seward paid 7.2 million dollars for a territory mocked as a frozen wasteland, a bargain at roughly two cents an acre. The Klondike gold rush three decades later made the mockery look foolish.
July 20, 1969 — Armstrong’s boot, a camera left behind to watch, and 600 million viewers.
April 1, 1976 — three founders; the first product was a bare circuit board.

November 11, 1918: the guns stopped on the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, and the celebrating hid how little the peace would hold. The war had unmade four empires and killed perhaps sixteen million people.
October 29, 1969 — "LO." The intended "LOGIN" crashed the system after two letters.
August 16, 1858: the new cable under the Atlantic carried 99 words of congratulation in an hour, plus celebration fireworks and parades, and then died within weeks. The 1866 cable stuck, and stayed.
January 1926: in a London attic, Baird showed a flickering human face to a Royal Institution audience. A decade later the world was watching broadcasts, and the flicker never stopped.
July 14, 1789: the great prison held seven inmates, four forgers, two madmen and a noble, but its gunpowder mattered. The king’s hunting diary for that day records a single word: nothing.
October 25, 1415, St. Crispin’s Day: mud, arrows, and a French charge that bogged down ankle-deep. Shakespeare gave the king a better speech than the field did, but not by much.

June 1314: a smaller Scottish army trapped the English cavalry in boggy ground between the Bannock and the Forth. The victory secured Scottish independence for a generation, though the formal treaty waited until 1328.
October 14, 1066. Harold died late in the day, and by Christmas a French-speaking duke was being crowned in Westminster.
May 7, 1824: the deaf man on stage could not hear the applause behind him until a singer turned him around to see it. The choral finale is now the anthem of Europe and the year-end ritual of Japan.

August 13, 1961: Sunday-morning Berlin woke to barbed wire across its streets. The wire stopped the exodus that was bankrupting the East; the concrete followed, and the city spent twenty-eight years learning to live around it.
November 9, 1989 — a botched press conference and guards who stopped taking orders.
1856: blowing cold air through molten iron burned away the carbon and made steel cheap enough to rail a continent. Bessemer retired rich; the American who had the same idea got little.
Autumn 1347, at Messina — within five years perhaps a third of the continent was gone.

September 7, 1822: the Portuguese prince told his father’s ministers no, with a sword, in a streambed near São Paulo. Brazil kept a crown and kept its unity while Spanish America broke into a dozen pieces.

May 24, 1883: the elder Roebling died of the caisson disease before a stone was laid, and his son was crippled by the same bends while his wife ran the site. Six days after the opening, a stampede on the bridge killed twelve people.

May 17, 1954: a unanimous court ended legal school segregation in nine paragraphs, overruling half a century of separate but equal. The case carried a Topeka welder’s name and was argued by the lawyer who would become the first Black justice.

January 24, 1848: a contractor checking a millrace found flakes the size of a thumbnail, and the man who owned the mill tried to keep it quiet. His whole work force walked off within weeks, and the forty-niners followed.

November 1532: fewer than two hundred men ambushed an emperor at a peaceful meeting and held him for the largest ransom in history. The Incas filled a room with gold, and the Spaniards killed him anyway.

January 1959: Batista fled at dawn on New Year’s Day, and Castro’s column took a week to walk the island’s length, cheered the whole way. The revolution’s turn toward the Soviet bloc came within two years.

May 6, 1994: an idea older than Napoleon finally connected, and the queen and the president opened it in person. Trains cross twenty-three miles of chalk in thirty-five minutes; the Victorians who tried first got two miles and lost the money.
December 25, 800. Pope Leo III set the crown on his head during the Mass, and Byzantium spent centuries refusing to applaud.
April 26, 1986 — the announcement began with Swedish monitors noticing radiation that wasn’t theirs.
September 6, 1522: the Victoria limped into Seville with fewer than 20 of the original crew, and without Magellan, who had died in the Philippines.

July 2, 1964: the filibuster lasted fifty-four working days and was broken by cloture, the first ever voted on a civil rights bill. Johnson signed with dozens of pens, and the public accommodations clause reached every lunch counter at once.
October 12, 1492 — an island in the Bahamas he insisted on calling the Indies.

February 1848: a pamphlet by two obscure Germans was a footnote to that year’s revolutions, printed in an edition too small to matter. Within a lifetime it was the most-printed political text on earth.
From late 1814 the powers danced through a year of balls and bargaining; the settlement they wrote kept Europe’s borders mostly quiet for a hundred years.
August 6, 2012 — the seven minutes of terror, a sky-crane hover, and it stuck the landing.
June 6, 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history, on five beaches and from the air.

September 1504: a block of marble two other sculptors had already abandoned lay weathering in a cathedral yard for decades before Michelangelo claimed it. The committee that chose its street corner included Leonardo and Botticelli.
Nuremberg, 1543: printed as he lay dying, it argued that Earth turns around the Sun. Nearly a century passed before Kepler and Galileo settled the argument in the book’s favor.
Philadelphia, July 4, 1776 — news crossed the Atlantic by sailing ship, weeks later.

December 1898: the Curies named the new element for the rays it gave off on its own. Marie Curie processed tonnes of pitchblende by hand to isolate a speck of it, and the work slowly cost her her life.

July 5, 1996: a lamb grown from a mammary cell carried DNA from one sheep, an egg from another and was carried by a third, so she had no father and three mothers. Named after Dolly Parton for the obvious reason, she stands stuffed in the National Museum of Scotland.

January 1605: the funny book about a mad knight sold out its first printing in weeks and made a broke old soldier the father of the modern novel. Part two followed a decade later and invented the sequel.

April 25, 1953: a single page in Nature proposed two backbones wound around each other. The photograph that settled the shape was made by Rosalind Franklin, who was not on the paper; she died at thirty-seven, four years before a Nobel she could not have been given.

April 22, 1970: twenty million people, a tenth of the country, came out for a teach-in a Wisconsin senator had staffed with twenty-somethings. The Environmental Protection Agency existed by the end of the year.

October 1879: after months of filament failures the lab’s carbon lamp burned for thirteen and a half hours. Newspapers called the inventor the wizard of Menlo Park, and lower Manhattan glowed on his wires within two years.
March 1889 — critics called it a "useless and monstrous" tower. It was meant to come down in 1909.

May 1, 1931: the steel went up at four and a half floors a week, and President Hoover switched the lights on from Washington. Built in fourteen months in a depression, it stood so empty that New Yorkers called it the Empty State Building.

July 1751: Diderot and d’Alembert set out to index every craft and idea in one alphabet; the engravers’ plates of the trades are now the best record of how things were made. The pope put it on the Index.
February 1946: thirty tons of tubes and switches computed a shell’s arc faster than the shell flew. The six women who programmed it by patch cable went unnamed for half a century.

January 1649: a king was beheaded outside his own banqueting house, by a court whose authority he refused to recognize. The monarchy and the House of Lords were abolished within weeks, and Britain became a republic for eleven years.
May 29, 1453: gunpowder finally beat the Theodosian Walls, Constantine XI died in the breach, and the city became Istanbul, capital of an empire that would rule from the Danube to the Nile.
April 30, 1975 — helicopters lifting off rooftops, the war’s most famous photograph taken from below.

August 13, 1521: the conquistadors took the lake city only because tens of thousands of indigenous enemies of the Aztecs helped them. The causeways became the streets of Mexico City, which still sinks.
March 6, 1836: the garrison was overrun before dawn, and Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie died with it. Remember the Alamo became the rally of the Texas Revolution, settled weeks later at San Jacinto.
September 4, 476: the teenage Romulus Augustulus was packed off to a pension in Campania, the regalia went east to Zeno, and a barbarian officer ruled Italy.
July 1099: after a five-week siege the crusaders took the city, and an armed pilgrimage had become a conquest. The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem lasted less than a century before Saladin took it back.
May 29, 1953: the ninth British expedition to the mountain was the one that stood on it. They spent about fifteen minutes on top, and left a hole in the snow for someone else to find.
April 1896 — 14 nations, no women athletes, and a marathon winner who became a Greek national hero.

May 1796: Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with matter from a milkmaid’s cowpox sore, later with smallpox itself, and the boy stayed well. The word vaccine descends from vacca, the Latin for cow.

July 1930: thirteen teams came, four of them from Europe after a fortnight at sea. The hosts beat Argentina 4-2 in the final, and the trophy was a French sculptor’s gold-plated idea of winged victory.
July–August 1914 — a Sarajevo assassination lit a fuse the whole alliance system had laid.
April 1861 — the bombardment lasted a day and a half; the war lasted four years.
May 6, 1954: on a windy Oxford track, Bannister ran a mile in 3:59.4 with two pacemakers. Doctors had called the barrier impossible; within weeks it was merely difficult.

October 1752: a Philadelphia printer’s newspaper letter described flying a kite into a thundercloud to show lightning was electricity. French experimenters had already confirmed his pointed-rod idea; the kite made the better story.
July 14, 1789 — seven prisoners freed, one revolution begun.
April 12, 1961: one lap of the Earth in 108 minutes, and a 27-year-old test pilot became the most famous man alive. The flight lasted a single morning, and it gave the Space Age its first hero.

June 1633: the old man in the dock had taught half the Tuscan court, and he was shown the instruments twice before he knelt. He said the earth stands still, and spent his last nine years under house arrest with the moons of Jupiter in his telescope.
January 1610: four little stars that shuffled around Jupiter broke the Earth-centered sky for good. Naming them the Medicean stars was politics; the orbits were physics.
January 30, 1948: shot on his way to a prayer meeting by a Hindu nationalist, a martyr at 78. His ashes went to the rivers of India; his fasting had already stopped a civil war.

1206: the man who had spent his youth enslaved and hunted was raised on a felt mat and given a new name, ruler of all who dwell in felt tents. Within twenty years his horsemen had taken most of the capitals of the known world.
January 18, 1871: proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors while Paris lay under siege, chosen as the spot so France would never forget.

March 6, 1957: the colony took the name of an old empire, and a prime minister who had been a political prisoner seven years earlier stood up in the parliament his jailers had built. Within a decade nearly all of Africa had followed.

May 27, 1937: some two hundred thousand people paid a nickel each to walk the span before a single car was allowed. The chief engineer’s safety net saved nineteen men, who called themselves the halfway to hell club.

September 14, 2015: two laser arms felt a shiver a ten-thousandth of a proton wide, from two black holes that had merged over a billion years earlier. Einstein had priced the effect a century before and doubted anyone would ever measure it.

May 1, 1851: the world’s first world’s fair, a glass house built of mass-produced parts in months, drew six million visitors in half a year. The profits founded Kensington’s museum quarter, which was the point.

Autumn 1845: a fungus reached Ireland and the food of millions rotted in the fields. In seven years about a million people died and two million emigrated, and the island never regained its population.
September 2 to 6, 1666, starting in a bakery in Pudding Lane. It consumed 13,000 houses and 87 churches, and it broke the plague year’s back.
November 5, 1605 — thirty-six barrels of gunpowder under Parliament.
Mainz, around 1455 — about 180 copies, and Europe was never private again.
A lawsuit from 1439 had already let slip the secret press; by 1440 he was back at Mainz, and fifteen years later the Bible changed everything.
December 27, 537: the dome Justinian’s architects floated over a ring of windows stunned pilgrims for a thousand years. It was the largest interior space on earth and it took five years to build.
August 1791: the richest colony in the Americas rose against slavery itself. Thirteen years of war ended with Haiti, the first Black republic, independent in 1804.

July 4, 2012: two rival detectors saw the same faint bump, forty-eight years after the Edinburgh physicist whose name it carries had proposed it. The man himself, eighty-three, was in the audience and was seen to weep.
May 6, 1937 — "Oh, the humanity!" — 97 people aboard; 62 survived.
April 1990 — its first images were blurry; a 1993 servicing mission gave it glasses.

August 1981: IBM built its PC from off-the-shelf parts and licensed the operating system from a young company called Microsoft. The clones that followed made the architecture universal, and the licensing made Microsoft rich.
June 1325, aged 21. By traditional count he covered some 75,000 miles across the Muslim world and beyond, several times Marco Polo’s route.

August 1947: the midnight handover came with borders drawn by a lawyer who had never been east of Paris, and some twelve million people moved within weeks. It was the largest migration in history, in the worst month of the year to be fleeing.

June 1812: more than half a million men crossed the Niemen, the largest army Europe had ever assembled. Fewer than one in ten came back; the retreat destroyed the myth of invincibility that had held the empire together.
June 29, 2007 — lines around Apple Stores; the App Store didn’t even exist until a year later.

May 1607: about a hundred colonists anchored on a marshy island in the James River and named the place for their king. The starving years that followed killed most of them, and the colony survived by learning to grow tobacco.
November 22, 1963 — the Zapruder film exists because a dressmaker brought his camera to Dealey Plaza.

March 17, 1861: a kingdom stitched from a dozen states was still missing Rome and Venice, and the new parliament simply declared the king of Sardinia king of Italy. Cavour, the man who had planned it, died three months later.
January 14, 1506: a farmer hit marble, and Michelangelo was sent to verify the find before the pope bought it. Michelangelo himself was accused of forging it.
1498: Leonardo painted a wall with the tempera technique of a panel and predicted it would fail; within twenty years the paint was flaking. It has been under repair more or less ever since.
October 7, 1571, in the Gulf of Patras: the Holy League’s galleys broke the Ottoman line in a single afternoon; a young Cervantes sailed in it and lost the use of his left hand.
April 1865: Lee surrendered at Appomattox on the 9th, and Lincoln was shot on the 14th. The war ended and the fight over its meaning began.
May 1927 — 33 and a half hours, dead reckoning, and a periscope because he couldn’t see past the fuel tank.

October 1935: some eighty-six thousand had left Jiangxi a year earlier; the column that reached Shaanxi was a fraction of that. The walk became the founding legend of the People’s Republic, and most of its leaders had made it on foot.
1803 — 828,000 square miles from Napoleon for about four cents an acre.
August 10, 1793, with 537 paintings on the walls, most of them confiscated from the crown. A palace became public property in an afternoon.

September 1519: five ships and about 270 men left Spain. One ship and 18 men returned three years later, without Magellan, who died in the Philippines, and the voyage proved the globe could be sailed around.
Runnymede, June 1215 — the king first put his seal under the law. He ignored it within weeks.
May 1994 — a fully representative election, four years after leaving prison.
1324: the king of Mali gave away so much gold on his way to Mecca that the price of the metal sagged in Cairo for years. One chronicler simply gave up trying to count his camels.

December 1620: after a brutal crossing and a winter that killed half of them, the survivors built a village on a bay where a Wampanoag settlement had stood, emptied by plague years before. Their compact for self-government was signed before anyone stepped ashore.

January 3, 1868: samurai from the southwest handed a fifteen-year-old emperor his ancestors’ powers back, then used them to build railways, conscripts and a national school system in a single generation.

February and March 1865: an abbot with a garden and arithmetic counted seven traits across twenty-nine thousand pea plants. The society’s minutes record no questions after either talk, and biology waited thirty-five years to notice.

April 1742: Handel staged his new oratorio for two Dublin charities, and the audience was asked to leave swords and hooped skirts at home so more people would fit. London took years to accept sacred words in a theatre, but the Hallelujah Chorus never left.

April 1795: the law fixed the metre as a ten-millionth of the earth’s quarter meridian, replacing every feudal perch and toise with an earth-sized standard. Two astronomers were still out measuring it through a war zone.
September 1821: eleven years of war ended not in a republic but in an empire led by the conservative general who had been sent to crush the rebellion. Iturbide’s throne lasted less than a year.

1905: a patent clerk in Bern published four papers that remade physics, covering light, atoms, time, and mass. Any one of them would have made a career; together they redirected the century’s science.
October 1908 — "any color so long as it is black" came later; the price kept falling instead.
Florence, about 1503 — he carried it with him for the rest of his life.

May 24, 1844: a biblical phrase tapped along thirty-eight miles of wire reached Baltimore in an instant, and Morse let a young girl choose it. Within a decade and a half a cable lay under the Atlantic.

Summer 325: some three hundred bishops gathered at the emperor’s summons to argue over a single Greek letter, the difference between like and same. The creed they issued still repeats that argument every Sunday.
August 1920 — 72 years after Seneca Falls, decided by one state legislator’s mother’s advice.
Wittenberg, October 1517 — the split that remade Europe began as a complaint about indulgences.
November 1859 — the first printing of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on day one.

August 15, 1914: the Ancon’s passage ended three decades in which a French company had gone bankrupt and an American president had taken a province to get the job done. Yellow fever was beaten before the canal was.
June 1381: Wat Tyler’s army camped on Blackheath, burned the duke of Lancaster’s palace, and met the boy king face to face at Mile End.
September 1928 — a stack of forgotten petri dishes, one careless summer, one lucky mold.

September 13, 1759: a short fight outside the city walls killed both generals within days of each other. France kept a shell of its empire in North America until 1763, when it handed nearly all of it to Britain.

November 1972: the test cabinet in a Sunnyvale bar broke because its coin slot had jammed solid with quarters. Two paddles and a square ball had built an industry, and the repair slip became video games’ first bug report.

January 1813: a parson’s daughter who had first drafted it as First Impressions at twenty sold it outright for one hundred and ten pounds and kept no copyright. The publishers have done rather better since.
1687, paid for out of Edmond Halley’s own pocket — the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

October 1863: a Swiss businessman who had seen the aftermath of Solferino called a conference to organize care for wounded soldiers, whoever they were. Every national society since has worn his city’s flag with the colors reversed.
May 1429: a teenage shepherd girl talked a king into an army and broke the longest siege of the war in nine days. The town’s bells have rung for her every May 8 since.
Spring 1848: barricades rose in a dozen capitals and kings ran for the coast. By autumn nearly everywhere had been rolled back, but nothing was quite the same.
December 1, 1955: her arrest began a 381-day boycott that carried a 26-year-old pastor named Martin Luther King Jr. onto the national stage.

July 1799: an officer of Napoleon’s expedition noticed a slab of black granite carrying hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek. Twenty-three years later Champollion read the top line, and Egypt’s sealed past opened.
July 1947 — a press release about a "flying disc," then a weather balloon, then fifty years of argument.

1662: a club of experimenters got a royal seal and, soon after, a motto that refuses to take anybody’s word for anything. Its journal, the Philosophical Transactions, is the oldest science journal still running.
April 1204: a crusade that never reached the Holy Land gutted Christendom’s greatest city instead, and the Venetians sailed home with its bronze horses.

March 12, 1930: a sixty-one-year-old in a homespun dhoti walked 240 miles to the sea and picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking the empire’s monopoly. Within a month the salt laws were publicly shattered down the whole coastline and sixty thousand people were in jail.
September 1, 1939 — the Luftwaffe hit Wieluń at 4:40 in the morning.
September 11, 2001 — the morning the towers fell and the century found its shape.
April 1564 — his actual birthday is unknown; the record is his baptism.

October 31, 1512: four years on scaffolding with his neck bent back and paint in his eyes, and he insisted he was no painter at all. The scaffolding came down two days later, and Rome has looked up ever since.

May 8, 1980: the disease that killed more people than every war combined was declared extinct after an eleven-year hunt for its last hiding places. The final natural case had been a hospital cook in Somalia, and he survived.
Brussels, October 1911: Einstein, Planck, Curie and Rutherford sat in one room to argue about quanta; the group photograph became the discipline’s academy portrait.
Summer 1588: 130 ships, unfavorable winds, fireships in the Calais roads, and North Sea storms that finished the job on the way home.
October 4, 1957 — a polished 58cm sphere that beeped at the whole world at once.
May 1703 — a new capital raised from a swamp, by imperial decree.

October 28, 1886: a French sculptor’s copper colossus rose on a pedestal paid for partly by schoolchildren’s coins after the rich refused. The fireworks went up through a fog so thick that only the harbor saw them.
September 1825 — Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first fare-paying passengers.
November 1869 — it cut the London-to-Bombay run by thousands of miles.
March 1876 — the same day he made the famous call to his assistant: "Mr. Watson, come here."

1960: a biology teacher and a philanthropist funded the research, a Catholic obstetrician ran the trials in Puerto Rico, and the regulators approved it in June. Sanger was in her eighties and had been demanding it since before women could vote.
April 15, 1912 — over 1,500 died in water just below freezing. The Californian never answered.
October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar: Nelson’s two columns cut the combined fleet apart, and he died below decks as the victory was sealed.
December 23, 1947: a sliver of germanium amplified without a filament or a vacuum. Bardeen and Brattain took a Nobel with their tempestuous group lead, and the invention quietly took everything else.

September 3, 1783: signed in Paris almost two years after the guns stopped at Yorktown, it gave the United States everything to the Mississippi River and fishing rights off Newfoundland, which the new country would soon need more than it knew.
July 16, 1945 — "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Oppenheimer said he thought of it later.
November 1922 — "wonderful things" glimpsed through a small breach by candlelight.

1088, by tradition: students hired the professors there, a reversal that has kept the rector student-elected ever since. The city has fed, taxed and quarreled with its scholars for nine centuries and counting.
October 1929 — Black Thursday, then Black Monday, then Black Tuesday, then a decade of it.
June 18, 1815 — four days later he abdicated; the exile to Saint Helena followed.

January 1769: a repair job on a lecture-hall model engine led an instrument maker to see that the waste was in the cooling itself. The patent he filed held the idea for a quarter century and powered the industrial revolution.

January 15, 2001: the serious encyclopedia project had been a failure, and its leftover volunteer pages were opened to anyone who showed up. A month later it had a thousand articles; the serious project closed with two dozen.

July 1877: twenty-two players paid a guinea each to enter, and the final was postponed three days so the gentry could watch the Eton and Harrow cricket match. Spencer Gore won it and called the whole game boring.
December 17, 1903 — four flights at Kitty Hawk; the longest lasted 59 seconds.

August 6, 1991: a physicist’s page about the web itself went up on a NeXT machine with a hand-written label warning not to power it down. CERN put the code into the public domain two years later and took no royalty on the invention of the age.

November 8, 1895: a Bavarian physicist noticed a screen glowing across the lab from a covered tube and spent weeks chasing the unknown ray in secret. His picture of his wife’s hand, ring and all, ran in every newspaper on earth.

July 1405: more than three hundred ships left the Longjiang yards under a Muslim eunuch admiral, some with crews counted in the hundreds. Seven voyages later the court lost interest and the ocean went quiet.
